newsitem.title: UK: POLL-Dagenham voters bored, baffled by UK election.
newsitem.headline: POLL-Dagenham voters bored, baffled by UK election.

text.p: It's 10.30 a.m. on a sunny spring morning. Theresa Jennings is thankful that it's not too chilly. She loiters on a busy street trying to catch the eye of passers-by, clipboard in hand.
Most dont give her the time of day.

But Jennings is not offering anything. Her task is more difficult than persuading you to sign up for some mail order catalogue or lend your support to charity. In Britain's longest ever election campaign, she wants election-weary voters to divulge their political preferences.

Political opinion polls have dominated the media over the last few weeks. While sometimes offering conflicting results, they provide the best possible indication of how the parties are faring in the run-up to the May 1 election.
But someone has to get out there and ask the questions.
Jennings was one of 52 interviewers doing the leg-work around Britain last Friday for a poll by NOP for Reuters news agency.
Standing on a busy street in Dagenham, south east England, Jennings tries to grab amenable-looking residents and persuade them to reveal their political leanings.

She must get a representative cross-section of people based on age, sex, working status and social grading. She tries to avoid couples, as men are usually dragged away by their eager-to-get-on-with-the-shopping wives.
Today is a good day. In less than five minutes she enlists the help of a 63-year-old lady pushing her grandchild in a pram.
But simply mentioning the election provokes a heated response.
"I'm not going to vote for no one," the woman declares. "No, no, no...none of them. They're all the same."

Dagenham, home to a huge Ford car plant, is a staunch Labour constituency. In the 1992 election, Labour reaped 52.3 percent of the votes compared with 36.3 percent for the Conservatives and 11.5 percent for the Liberal Democrats.
So many residents have no doubt where they'll put their cross on polling day.
"If Labour dont get in then I'll shoot myself," said one man, laughing.

The survey takes three to four minutes and respondents are bombarded with questions. Which party would you vote for? Which party do you trust most to manage the economy? Which party do you trust most to manage Britain's relations with Europe? Who would make you better off?
Some get a bit fed up.
"Labour, Labour, Labour, LABOUR," said one man, his voice rising with impatience.
But the mood in the air is that people, in Dagenham at least, have already had enough of the election.

The prospect of a televised debate between the party leaders provoked little excitement, while the sex and money allegations which have rocked the Conservative party over recent weeks were met with rolled eyes and sighs.
"They're all at it, aren't they?," said one man. "Not like us. We're all squeaky clean," he said, winking at the Reuters reporter who observed the interviews.
"People shouldn't take notice of all that sex and all that. It's not about what they done in their private lives, is it?" said another, younger, voter.

Economic issues, while crucial for financial markets, just confuse ordinary voters. Taxes have fallen, employment has risen and inflation appears to be under control, but the Dagenham electorate was reluctant to give the Conservatives the credit.
"What we've paid out under the Tories has gone up and up. But you have to decide between the devil you know and the devil you dont," said a retired train driver.
Some voters feel passionately about certain issues, although not enough to switch allegiance from one party to another.
"I'd say the Liberal Democrats would manage the economy well, but that's just a wasted vote in this borough," said one.
"I should vote for the Referendum party because they'd get us out of bloody Europe," said another.

After the first hour, Jennings' refusal rate was only 50 percent and she had half the 20 replies she needed. But her task was set to get more difficult as she strove to match the respondents with her quota.
So she ploughed on as the lunch hour neared, bringing the chance of more people on the streets.
"Excuse me, but are you 34 or under?" she asked as she approached one woman. No, she was 36. "No good for my quota, but I probably made her day," Jennings laughed.

The biggest worry for some respondents was their lack of political knowledge. Public opinion surveys attempt to gauge how the public would vote but they are faced with respondents who often know little about the issues at stake.
"I dont know a lot about politics. I talk about it, but if I had to go to a meeting or anything -- blimey," said an elderly retired hospital cleaner.
Jennings tried not to put words into people's mouths, but sometimes respondents needed help.
"Who will win? Maybe it will be...what do you call them? Who's in now?"
People also stumbled over the way questions were phrased.
Asked the very first question, which party would she vote for "if there were a general election tomorrow", one woman panicked.
"Is the election tomorrow?" she gasped.
